title: A Proposed Rule Could End the 'Day 1 CPT' Lifeline That Thousands of Indian Graduates Depend On
excerpt: The Trump administration wants to restrict repeat degree enrolments used to maintain work authorisation. Immigration attorneys warn the move could push thousands of Indian tech workers out of the country.
body:
For thousands of Indian graduates working in the United States, a second or third master's degree was never really about education. It was about staying legal.

The practice, widely known as "Day 1 CPT" (Curricular Practical Training), has quietly become one of the most important — and most controversial — immigration workarounds in America's tech corridor. Indian professionals who lose the annual H-1B visa lottery enrol in another academic programme, often at a for-profit or low-residency university, to maintain their work authorisation through CPT while continuing to hold full-time technology jobs.

Now, a proposed rule from the Trump administration threatens to shut that door. And immigration attorneys say the impact on the Indian tech workforce could be severe.

## What the Rule Would Change

The proposed regulation targets the F-1 student visa framework in two ways. First, it would impose stricter requirements on what counts as a valid academic programme eligible for CPT, effectively disqualifying repeat enrolments in overlapping fields of study. A software engineer who already holds a master's degree in computer science would not be able to enrol in another technology-related master's programme purely to maintain work authorisation.

Second, the rule would cut the grace period available to F-1 students after their legal status ends from 60 days to 30 days — halving the window in which a graduate can secure alternative visa sponsorship or make plans to leave the country.

## Why This Hits Indians Hardest

Indians account for roughly 75 per cent of all H-1B visa approvals. But the lottery system means that even highly qualified candidates face multiple years of rejection. Federal data has shown that some individuals were registered by employers up to 83 times in a single fiscal year, and over 9,000 people had more than five registrations each — evidence of widespread gaming by staffing firms that has triggered a regulatory backlash.

For those who play by the rules and still lose the lottery year after year, Day 1 CPT has been the fallback. According to immigration attorney Tahmina Watson, tens of thousands of Indian nationals working in AI, machine learning, software engineering and data science currently rely on this pathway.

"For anyone who already has a master's degree, they are not going to be able to go back and say, 'I need another master's degree because I need work authorisation to continue working,'" said Kathleen Goldman, a partner at a major immigration law firm, in comments to The Indian Eye.

## The Ripple Effect on Employers

The proposed change does not only affect students. Goldman warned that U.S. companies — already struggling to fill specialised roles — would face a talent squeeze if existing immigration pathways become more restrictive.

"There's no doubt about it that this is going to have a massive impact on the companies that are in desperate need of top talent," she said. Foreign nationals make up a substantial portion of America's AI talent pool, and losing them would force companies to either scale back or shift operations overseas.

Some firms may pivot to cap-exempt H-1B programmes available at universities and non-profit research institutions, or turn to O-1 visas reserved for individuals with extraordinary ability. But those routes are narrower, more expensive, and not available to the average mid-career engineer.

## A Broader Crackdown

The student visa proposal is one piece of a larger immigration overhaul. In September 2025, Trump signed a proclamation imposing a $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions — a measure that priced out many staffing firms and mid-tier contractors that had been the biggest sponsors of Indian workers. The Department of Housing and Urban Development barred non-permanent residents from accessing FHA-insured mortgages starting May 2025, contributing to a housing market correction in Indian-heavy suburbs of Dallas.

Meanwhile, Representative Chip Roy of Texas this week introduced the American White-Collar Worker Jobs Act of 2026, which would replace the H-1B lottery with a wage-based selection process and — in its most radical provision — end the use of H-1B visas as a pathway to permanent residency altogether, while eliminating the OPT programme that allows foreign students to work after graduation.

Taken together, the measures represent the most aggressive restructuring of legal immigration pathways since the H-1B programme was created nearly forty years ago.

## What Comes Next

The proposed F-1 rule is in the public comment period. If finalised, it would take effect in the coming months. For Indian families who have built careers, bought homes and raised children in the United States on the assumption that legal pathways would remain open, the uncertainty is acute.

"The companies will either struggle because they won't have the talent or they will have to get creative and find alternate solutions," Goldman said. For the tens of thousands of Indians caught between a visa lottery they cannot win and a CPT door that may be closing, creative solutions are already running out.

**Sources:** The Indian Eye, NY Post, LiveMint, Nagaland Post (IANS), Reuters
